profiles.author: Bessel van der Kolk
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against the listed claim-mapped sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. publication.basis: Original work dated 2014; bibliographic and publisher sources in this profile concern original release or specific example editions, not an owned copy.

profiles.genre_and_form: Popular nonfiction; trauma, psychiatry and treatment history
profiles.summary: Van der Kolk recounts how clinical approaches to psychological trauma developed and argues that traumatic experiences can persist in embodied patterns of arousal, memory, attention and interpersonal response. Case histories and treatment stories give the book narrative urgency, but its evocative organizing metaphor should not be mistaken for one established diagnostic mechanism.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Published in 2014, The Body Keeps the Score combines the author’s clinical career, patient narratives and interpretations of neuroscientific studies with a strong preference for wider models of trauma treatment. Its influence in popular culture is substantial. Later independent commentary has disputed how confidently some broad neurobiological claims and body-oriented interventions follow from the available evidence.
profiles.before_reading: Read with two pencils, figuratively: one for the experiences and ethical questions that ring true in the case narratives, another for specific claims about brain changes or comparative therapy efficacy. The VA/DoD 2023 guideline prioritizes several trauma-focused approaches; do not treat this book as a personalized treatment plan.
profiles.literary_approach: The book moves between individual stories, the history of psychiatric diagnosis, explanations of brain/body processes and practical suggestions. That alternation helps readers retain compelling anecdotes but can blur the level of evidence behind a generalization. Track whether a passage describes a single case, a correlational finding, a randomized study or an author recommendation.
profiles.context: This is a clinician-authored interpretive synthesis, not a recent systematic review of PTSD interventions. The book’s public legacy includes both advocacy for trauma-informed care and later pointed criticism of selected empirical claims. Evaluating it carefully means neither dismissing testimony nor assuming a persuasive metaphor settles comparative treatment questions.

publication.basis: Original work dated 1971; bibliographic and publisher sources in this profile concern original release or specific example editions, not an owned copy.

profiles.genre_and_form: Literary fantasy; Earthsea cycle, book two

series.name: Earthsea
series.sequence_status: Read after A Wizard of Earthsea to notice changes in perspective, but the user may choose another order.

profiles.summary: A girl taken from her family becomes a high priestess within a secluded labyrinthine religious institution, where the name imposed on her is part of a demand for total allegiance. Her meeting with an outsider tests what obedience, belonging and selfhood could mean. This introduction deliberately avoids describing the outcome or future Earthsea relationships.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Le Guin published The Tombs of Atuan in book form with Atheneum in 1971 after an earlier shorter magazine appearance, and it became the second Earthsea title. Unlike a simple sequel centered entirely on the wizard Ged, this novel places the young priestess Tenar near the narrative center and narrows attention to ritual, architecture and the experience of being assigned a destiny.
profiles.before_reading: Notice who can enter a room, who knows a true name and who controls the maps. The atmosphere is often claustrophobic: the Tombs are not only a setting but a system that teaches its inhabitants which questions cannot be asked. Consider the book’s view of religious authority without prejudging each character’s reasons for loyalty.
profiles.literary_approach: Le Guin uses a constrained setting, withheld light, carefully placed silence and controlled changes in point of view. In contrast with the geographical motion of A Wizard of Earthsea, the novel derives suspense from tight spatial knowledge and small decisions that may carry enormous moral consequences. The apparently simple prose is unusually disciplined.
profiles.context: The book belongs to an expanding fantasy cycle and to a broader literary conversation about the cost of enforced roles. Its depiction of ritual and subordination can be read as an inquiry into institutions rather than an easy equation of all faith with coercion. Publication-format differences should be checked against the edition actually read.

profiles.possible_mismatch: Readers expecting constant epic action may find its intentionally narrow setting and measured pace subdued.

profiles.author: Ivan Turgenev
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against the listed claim-mapped sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. publication.basis: Original work dated 1862; bibliographic and publisher sources in this profile concern original release or specific example editions, not an owned copy.

profiles.genre_and_form: Russian realist novel of ideas; generational and ideological conflict
profiles.summary: Arkady returns to his family home with Bazarov, a confident young man whose hostility to inherited ideals unsettles an older generation. Discussions of art, science, love and authority become a social laboratory in which people are more complicated than their chosen intellectual labels. The novel refuses to make the friction between affection and principle easy.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Fathers and Sons was published in Russian in 1862 amid contentious debates over reform and social authority. The novel’s portrayal of the “nihilist” Bazarov sparked disagreement about Turgenev’s own sympathies. An Oxford World’s Classics version translated and edited by Richard Freeborn draws on a later-discovered working manuscript; that fact alone does not make all translations identical or identify the reader’s edition.
profiles.before_reading: Keep a small note of which arguments characters defend in conversation and how they behave when disappointed or frightened. Watch the difference between a generation being genuinely wronged and an individual insisting that intellectual certainty cancels human attachment. Avoid reading Bazarov as simply the author’s mouthpiece.
profiles.literary_approach: Turgenev builds a novel of ideas through domestic encounters, visits and conversations rather than through a single philosophical manifesto. His tonal control and ironic juxtaposition allow the drama to test theories of social improvement against awkward particulars of family, illness and romantic feeling. Translation choices can change the feel of argument, irony and tenderness.
profiles.context: The novel emerges from the social and intellectual ferment surrounding emancipation and the Russian reform era. “Nihilism” here is a contested social identity, not a settled philosophical definition. Modern editions offer materially different translation and editorial apparatus; cite a translator explicitly when comparing language with other readers.

publication.basis: Original work dated 1988; bibliographic and publisher sources in this profile concern original release or specific example editions, not an owned copy.

series.name: Discworld — Wizards/Rincewind
series.sequence_status: This follows The Colour of Magic and The Light Fantastic in the selected strand; manual reordering always remains allowed.

profiles.summary: An impossibly potent wizard upends the rather institutional traditions of Unseen University, transforming a joke about academic authority into a dangerous test of what magic is allowed to become. Rincewind’s tendency to survive by fleeing provides a comic counterpoint to the temptation to treat raw power as an intellectual achievement.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Terry Pratchett estate dates Sourcery to May 26, 1988. It comes after the opening Rincewind adventures in the Discworld sequence and expands the satire beyond travelogue into university politics and magical ambition. Publisher and estate bibliographies distinguish the original publication from later paperback and illustrated reissues.
profiles.before_reading: Keep an eye on who gains status by talking grandly about power, and who suffers when that talk becomes literal. Some comic business deliberately exaggerates fantasy conventions from earlier books. The queue is yours to reorder; if you start here, be prepared for characters with established histories.
profiles.literary_approach: Pratchett uses comic reversals, mock-formal language and sudden changes in scale, shifting from academic petty disputes to a fantasy threat. The humor continually punctures categories such as wise wizard, prophesied hero and respectable institution; beneath the gags runs an inquiry into the political uses of exceptional talent.
profiles.context: Early Discworld works are both fantasy parodies and a developing social satire; Sourcery belongs to the period in which the fictional world acquires increasingly distinct institutions. This profile avoids spoilers for the full conflict and for subsequent Rincewind novels.

profiles.author: Nadine Burke Harris
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against the listed claim-mapped sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. publication.basis: Original work dated 2018; bibliographic and publisher sources in this profile concern original release or specific example editions, not an owned copy.

series.name: Standalone
series.sequence_status: No required sequence; the title is a suggested book.

profiles.summary: Pediatrician Nadine Burke Harris writes about the relationship between difficult childhood experiences, later health and the responsibilities of clinicians and communities. By combining stories from clinical practice with the emerging public-health language of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), the book makes an argument for taking social context seriously in pediatric care.
profiles.author_and_work_background: First published in 2018 by Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, The Deepest Well helped introduce wider audiences to ACE research and pediatric screening. Subsequent methodological literature argues that ACE counts are useful for describing population patterns but not a precise diagnosis or prognosis for an individual child. It is important to distinguish the author’s advocacy and case narratives from validated interventions.
profiles.before_reading: Approach the science with a compassionate but non-deterministic lens. Risk correlations do not predict what will happen to a particular person, and resilience and protective relationships matter. Do not calculate a personal ACE total and interpret it as medical destiny; follow any health decisions with qualified clinical care.
profiles.literary_approach: The book braids practitioner memoir, specific clinical vignettes, epidemiologic explanations and appeals for system change. Moving from a patient’s vivid story to a population-level association is rhetorically effective but also a place where readers should slow down and ask what causal inference is justified.
profiles.context: The modern ACEs literature is large and frequently misapplied. Research critiques emphasize that a simple count omits severity, duration, timing and positive childhood experiences, and cannot determine treatment eligibility. The book is valuable as a history of a public-health argument without being a substitute for current practice guidelines.

profiles.possible_mismatch: Accounts of childhood trauma may be distressing; rapid shifts among story, mechanism and policy are not always easy to independently verify.

profiles.title: The Myth of Sisyphus
profiles.author: Albert Camus
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against the listed claim-mapped sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. Clinical/self-help arguments are not patient-level guidance. Not an exhaustive scene audit or verification of owned ISBN, page count, audio duration, cover or every possible content concern.

publication.basis: Original work dated 1942; bibliographic and publisher sources in this profile concern original release or specific example editions, not an owned copy.

series.name: Camus — cycle of the absurd
series.sequence_status: The essay is a standalone philosophical commitment; related creative works need not be read first.

profiles.summary: Camus begins from the confrontation between the human longing for meaning and a world that does not supply a reassuring answer. In a tightly argued, rhetorically charged essay he tests whether lucidity about that predicament entails despair, then turns toward an ethic of continued living and revolt. The final Sisyphus image is a challenge to easy consolations rather than a claim that suffering is pleasant.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Myth of Sisyphus appeared in French in 1942 as part of Camus’s planned “absurd” grouping alongside The Stranger and Caligula. English editions include Justin O’Brien’s translation, with later publishers adding different editorial introductions or afterwords. Camus’s relation to existentialism is disputed and should not be collapsed into Sartre’s doctrines.
profiles.before_reading: Do not skim from the opening question straight to the famous final image. Identify what Camus means by “the absurd” in each stage and distinguish philosophical suicide, literal suicide, revolt and consolation. His argument is not a health guide and should not be read as advice in a crisis.
profiles.literary_approach: The prose blends conceptual distinctions, literary portraits, examples and mythic imagery. Rather than offering a formal deductive system, Camus moves dialectically, asking what conclusions follow if one refuses both religious comfort and philosophical escape. Translation matters especially where concise French philosophical vocabulary is rendered with loaded English terms.
profiles.context: Written under the pressure of wartime Europe, the essay belongs to philosophical debates over nihilism, existentialism and moral agency. The Stanford Encyclopedia explains both its historical pairing with Camus’s fiction and why later interpreters resist treating Camus as simply another Sartrean existentialist.

profiles.possible_mismatch: The subject of suicide is explicit, and the non-systematic essay style can feel slippery without active note-taking.

profiles.genre_and_form: Literary fantasy; Earthsea cycle, book three

series.name: Earthsea
series.sequence_status: Third Earthsea book; plot and character perspective build on prior works, but manual reading order is free.

profiles.summary: As magic appears to diminish in distant parts of Earthsea, a young prince joins a great wizard to learn what has disturbed the fabric of their world. The journey crosses seas and beliefs as much as geography, asking whether fear of loss can deform the very practices that make life meaningful. The profile omits the solution and later Earthsea developments.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Ursula K. Le Guin’s estate documents an Atheneum first publication in 1972 and positions The Farthest Shore third in the Earthsea sequence. It follows A Wizard of Earthsea and The Tombs of Atuan while broadening the canvas from apprenticeship and enclosure toward death, social order and the limits of mastery.
profiles.before_reading: Attend to how people describe the loss of magic rather than deciding immediately what causes it. A prince’s inexperienced viewpoint can be useful because his questions invite readers to scrutinize the authority of those he admires. Keep future-book summaries closed if you wish to avoid spoilers.
profiles.literary_approach: Le Guin structures the novel as a voyage: successive islands reveal new versions of the same disturbance, creating thematic recurrence rather than a simple collection of episodic adventures. Restrained description, significant names and the motif of boundaries give the final third of the initial Earthsea sequence a meditative weight.
profiles.context: Le Guin’s fiction regularly examines the relation between freedom, balance, mortality and power. The Farthest Shore should not be reduced to a single allegory: its death-consciousness interacts with character growth, environmental imagery and the obligations of rule. Specific maps and illustrations can vary across later editions.

publication.basis: Original work dated 1890; bibliographic and publisher sources in this profile concern original release or specific example editions, not an owned copy.

profiles.genre_and_form: Gothic philosophical novel; Victorian aestheticism and moral fable

series.name: Standalone
series.sequence_status: Required literary classic; flexible placement in ordinary queue.

profiles.summary: A young man becomes preoccupied with preserving youth and beauty while his portrait appears to reflect a widening separation between his public image and private conduct. Wilde turns an apparently supernatural premise into an unsettling examination of influence, performance, temptation and conscience. The setup poses an ethical question without revealing the end of Dorian’s story.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Wilde’s only novel appeared in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine in 1890, followed by an expanded book edition in 1891. The Morgan Library documents six new chapters and significant revisions. Modern scholarly editors have also reconstructed an uncensored manuscript-based text; a reader must choose between materially different textual objects rather than treating “the original” as one unambiguous edition.
profiles.before_reading: Decide which text you are reading before comparing chapter numbers, descriptions or quotations with a discussion group. Observe how aphorisms sound simultaneously brilliant and dangerous depending on who believes them. The novel rewards attention to social pressure and the gap between elegance of style and reliability of moral judgment.
profiles.literary_approach: Wilde mixes epigrammatic dialogue with Gothic mystery and a carefully managed portrait motif. The narrator’s handling of the fantastic is restrained enough that a moral drama can proceed through conversation and consequence. Revisions across manuscript, magazine and 1891 book complicate any claim that one sentence transparently speaks for Wilde’s final intention.
profiles.context: The book’s Victorian controversy cannot be separated from debates over aestheticism, sexuality, censorship and respectable public identity. The British Library and Morgan archives document its reception and textual development; their findings establish historical change, not a single mandatory moral interpretation of the novel.

profiles.genre_and_form: Relationship self-help; popular presentation of adult attachment research

series.name: Standalone
series.sequence_status: Optional suggestion; not part of required classics/philosophy set.

profiles.summary: Psychiatrist Amir Levine and Rachel Heller introduce readers to a three-style scheme for understanding intimacy, conflict and reassurance in romantic relationships. Exercises and scenarios turn a research tradition into concrete dating advice. That clarity is useful for starting conversations, but the typology is an interpretive simplification rather than a permanent diagnostic label for a person.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The original work dates to late 2010 in Tarcher/Penguin publishing records; later paperback and audio pages have their own publication dates. The book draws from attachment theories historically associated with Bowlby and adult romantic researchers. Independent research generally measures adult attachment in at least the dimensions of anxiety and avoidance instead of assuming everyone fits neatly into three stable, mutually exclusive types.
profiles.before_reading: Use the book’s examples to articulate needs and patterns, not to decide a partner’s worth or personality category. Observe the situation, relationship, stressors and behavior before invoking a type label. Neither a self-report style questionnaire nor a popular-science book diagnoses a mental disorder or proves the motives of someone else.
profiles.literary_approach: Attached is structured around recognizable relationship stories, explanatory categories and repeatable exercises. The authors’ clean types create memorable narrative arcs, while the stronger underlying social-psychology literature measures patterns that vary by context and relationship. Mark the difference between “this example resembles my experience” and a prediction warranted by controlled studies.
profiles.context: Attachment theory offers useful questions about security, closeness and stress regulation. Its findings do not justify deterministic predictions of a couple’s future, amateur diagnoses or a refusal to consider material circumstances. Work by Fraley and others documents the dimensional and measurement issues obscured by quick “style” quizzes.

profiles.genre_and_form: Comic fantasy parody; illustrated Discworld/Rincewind story

series.name: Discworld — Wizards/Rincewind
series.sequence_status: Later Rincewind episode; reader may deliberately reorder the normal queue.

profiles.summary: An ambitious young would-be magician attempts to summon a demon and instead draws the luckless Rincewind into a parody of the Faust tradition. Wishes and grand ambitions collide with bureaucratic, literal-minded absurdity. The joke grows from asking what power would actually deliver to a person who has thought very little about consequences.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Originally published by Victor Gollancz in 1990, Eric has an unusual edition history: the large-format original involved Josh Kirby’s illustrations, while later text-only and illustrated reissues are not visual duplicates. Colin Smythe’s bibliographic record is particularly useful for distinguishing the formats. This is an intentional parody of the Faust bargain rather than an entry point to the entire Discworld mythology.
profiles.before_reading: If your copy has illustrations, give them attention as narrative contributions rather than decoration; if it does not, do not assume you have lost chapters. Be prepared for Rincewind’s ongoing misfortunes and for jokes that turn on the gap between an apparently impressive wish and its practical consequences.
profiles.literary_approach: Pratchett compresses a Faustian narrative into brisk comic scenes, deliberately literal interpretations and escalating collisions between desire and outcome. Visual editions add another layer of timing and grotesque exaggeration through Kirby’s art. A work-level description cannot confirm the arrangement or presence of illustrations in the reader’s own copy.
profiles.context: Faust stories traditionally dramatize bargains for knowledge, power or pleasure; Pratchett reduces the heroic solemnity and makes the transaction comically petty and institutional. The book belongs to the wider Discworld series and the Rincewind line, but its particular publishing history should be checked before comparing covers or audiobook editions.
